script.text: Monday, April 7
My alarm goes off at 5:40.
I'm usually awake before it. I lie there for the full ten seconds anyway, as a matter of principle, listening to the house.
The water heater ticking. A crow on the power line. Nothing from downstairs.
Second year of high school starts today. It doesn't feel like anything starts. It feels like Monday.
I get up.

The rice was on the timer last night, so the kitchen already smells like steam. Eggs, the leftover spinach, the last of the frozen {karaage|fried chicken}. Two lunch boxes, side by side on the counter.
I've gotten fast at this. Fast enough to do it while reading the whiteboard on the fridge.
Kendo: Monday, Wednesday, Friday and Saturday morning. Hoshino Kitchen: Tuesday, Thursday and Sunday. A red circle around the 18, Akane's clinic day. All of it in my handwriting.
All of it except the bottom line, which still says "Garbage: burnables, Mon/Thu" in Dad's. He wrote it last spring. I've never written over it.
The {fusuma|sliding door} to Mom's room is closed. It usually is.
"Morning, Onii-chan…"
My sister shuffles in already dressed for school, eyes still at half-mast.
"Morning. How'd you sleep?"
"Geez, Onii-chan! Every single morning!"
"And?"
"And I slept! Super well! I didn't wake up once!"
I look at her anyway. Color's fine. She isn't leaning on the doorframe. She isn't holding her head the way she does when the room starts tilting on her.
"Onii-chan, you're hovering again."
"I'm standing in my own kitchen."
"Then go hover over the eggs!"
"There's an egg with your name on it."
"Yaaay. …I could make my own lunch, you know."
"I'm already making two."
"…You always are."
She says it to the rice cooker, not to me. I pretend I didn't hear that.
The back door slides open. No knock. There's never a knock.
"Good morning. I'm coming in."
"You're already in."
"Then I've arrived. Good morning, Akane-chan."
"Morning, Nanoha-chan!"
She sets a plastic container on the table.
"{Kinpira|braised burdock}. Mom made too much again."
"Again."
"Again. She can't measure burdock. It's a sickness."
She's been bringing food over for about a year now. I used to argue. Somewhere around last summer, I gave up.
"Tell her thanks."

She goes to the cupboard left of the sink, the one with the mugs and not the one with the glasses, and takes down two without looking. She bumps the drawer under the counter with her hip so it won't stick. She reaches over the sink and jiggles the window latch at the exact angle it needs, so the steam can get out.
She's been doing all of that since she was tall enough to reach.
Which, considering it's Nanoha, wasn't that long ago.
"I heard that."
"I didn't say anything."
"You thought it in a short-person direction."
"He totally did."
"Traitor."
"Nanoha-chan brought kinpira!"
I wrap the lunches. I knock twice on the fusuma.
"Mom, we're heading out. There's rice in the cooker and miso soup on the stove. Just heat it up."
Nothing.
Then a small shift of weight on the other side of the paper. A creak of floorboard.
That's an answer. Sort of.
The path to school follows the river for a while before it turns toward town.

This week it's the best walk in Shirasawa. The cherry trees along the embankment are in full bloom, so heavy with flowers the branches sag over the path, and every time the wind comes down off the mountains the whole tunnel lets go at once.

Up on the hill above it all, where the shrine is, the Ōzakura is blooming too: one cherry tree older than anyone's records, so big that from the bridge it looks like a pink cloud caught on the hillside.
Nanoha walks on the river side.
"Now then. Class assignments."
"They'll be posted at the entrance."
"That's the boring answer. I've prepared a theory."
"Of course you have."
"There are six second-year classes. On paper, our odds of being in the same one are one in six."
"However. We've been in the same class four years running. A teacher somewhere has noticed. A file has been opened. There have been meetings."
"Meetings."
"In a small room with no windows. They've realized that if we're separated, something terrible happens. The school's feng shui collapses. The pool turns green."
"The pool is green."
"Because last year they put you in 1-C for five days during the exchange program. You remember."
"That was a scheduling error."
"That's what it says in the minutes."
I laugh.
"You laughed. That's two points for me this morning."
"We're keeping score now?"
"We've always been keeping score. You're losing."
A gust shakes the trees. Petals come down all at once, thick enough to lose the path in. One lands on her braid.
I don't mention it. It suits her.
"Kō-chan. Your collar."
Before I can do anything about it, she's in front of me, folding my shirt collar back down over my tie.
Her hands stay a second longer than they strictly need to.
"There. Now you look like someone who has his life together."
"…Thanks."
We walk on.
"Practice today?"
"Club doesn't start until Wednesday. First week."
"And after that?"
"Monday, Wednesday, Friday, Saturday morning. Shifts Tuesday, Thursday, Sunday."
"I know."
"Then why'd you ask?"
"So you'd hear yourself say it."
"It's fine. Saturday afternoons are free."
"Mm."
A few steps of nothing. The river is loud this time of year, fat with spring rain off the Tanzawa Mountains.
"Oh. Grandpa says the shrine's cherries are the best they've been in years. I'm helping him sweep up there Saturday."
"His back again?"
"His back is a very convenient back. It only hurts on days with a lot of petals."
"I'll come after practice. Somebody has to carry the trash bags while you supervise."
"I do supervise beautifully."
She walks a little faster after that, and for a while I actually have to work to keep up.
The entrance hall is chaos. Two hundred students trying to read six sheets of paper at once.
"Nano-chaaaan!"
A blur with pigtails and a cluster of novelty hair clips hits Nanoha from the side.
"Two-B! You're in Two-B! I'm in Two-B! It's destiny! It's in the stars! I'm making us matching keychains!"
"Good morning, Rika-chan."
Today's clips are a strawberry, a star and a small frog wearing a crown. The frog is new.
"And you walked in with Fujisawa-kun. Hm. Hmmm."
"What's 'hmmm'?"
"Nothing! Nothing! I'm just humming! Hmm-hmm-hmmm!"
"—which is why the correct way to eat a {taiyaki|fish-shaped cake} is head first."
Tokiwa has arrived the way he usually does, in the middle of an argument nobody else knew had started.
"Good morning, Tokiwa."
"The head has the most bean paste. You eat the best part while it's still hot, and the tail cleans your palate. That isn't an opinion. It's thermodynamics."
"It's seven-fifty in the morning."
"Tail first! You save the best part for last! Everybody knows that!"
"Then by the time you get there, it's cold."
"…Oh no."
"We'll resume this at lunch. I'll need a diagram."
"Please don't."
"Oh! Oh oh oh, but have you heard? Two-B is getting a transfer student!"
"A transfer student?"
"A girl! From somewhere! Far!"
"'Somewhere far' covers most of the planet."
"Then we've already narrowed it down!"
While they argue, I squeeze toward the board. I don't make it. Nanoha has already slipped through to the front and is pointing up at a line I can't see yet.
"Fujisawa Kōhei. Two-B. About halfway down."
"You found mine before yours?"
"Yours was easier. It's always right under Fukuda-kun's. Fukuda-kun is easy to find."
When I finally get to the board, Fukuda's not in Two-B this year. He's in Two-E. She went looking for mine before her own.
I don't know why that's the thing that sticks with me all through the opening ceremony.
I end up in the second-to-last row by the window. Nanoha's two rows over, which by the standards of the conspiracy is apparently acceptable. Tokiwa's near the front, already drawing his diagram.
Ōno-sensei, our homeroom teacher, shuffles in with the attendance sheet and the expression of a man who was born in a cardigan.
"All right. Settle down. Before we start—as some of you have apparently already heard, through channels I'd like to know more about—we have a new student joining us this year."
"Come on in."
The door opens.
She walks to the front of a room full of strangers like she's stepping onto a floor she's already won on.
Her hair falls long, in soft waves, brushed until it shines. Her uniform looks like it was ironed by someone who meant it.
"I'm Mizuno Natsuki. It's nice to meet you all."
"My dad's job moves us around a lot, so I've been the new girl…"
"…six times now? So please don't go easy on me."
A ripple of laughter. Someone in the front row actually claps.
"I do kendo, and I'm looking for a dojo that'll put up with me. I also love horror movies, the cheesier the better, so if anyone wants to watch a bad one with me, come find me."
Her eyes go along the rows while she says it. Then they get to me.
Her grin stutters. Just for a second. Just long enough that I'm sure I'm the only one who sees it.
"Looking forward to this year."
She bows, and the class gives her the friendly kind of applause.
I realize I've been holding my pen hard enough to hurt.
"Thank you, Mizuno. Let's see… the empty seat behind Fujisawa, by the window. Fujisawa, raise your hand so she doesn't have to wander."
I raise my left hand. She walks down the aisle.
When she passes my desk, she slows down just enough to lean in.
"Hey. Kendo, right?"
"…How did you—"
"Left palm. You've got the callus right where the {tsuka|hilt} sits. It takes years to get it that thick."
I look down at my hand like it's betrayed me.
"Takes one to know one."
And then she's past me, settling into the seat at my back, and I can feel the whole classroom's attention swing toward the window like a weathervane.
I keep my eyes on the board for the entire first period.

By lunch, Mizuno Natsuki has learned the names of half the class, answered "Sendai, most recently" about twenty times, been invited to two clubs, and agreed to go to karaoke with a group of girls whose names I don't think I've ever said out loud.
I've barely gotten the lid off my lunch when a chair scrapes behind me.
"So. You're Fujisawa."
"That's what the attendance sheet says."
"The guy who turned down three confessions last year."
I put my chopsticks down.
"Who told you that?"
"The girl by the door, before I'd even put my shoes in my locker."
"Great."
"She said you told all three of them you didn't have time for a girlfriend. True?"
"It's true that I don't have time."
"Huh."
She props her chin on her hand and looks me over. Shoulders. Hands. Like she's working out my reach.
"Do you always sit this straight?"
"What are you, {shodan|first dan}?"
"We'll find out on the floor."
"Big talk for someone who sits like he's being graded."
"Club starts Wednesday."
"Wednesday."
She takes a ballpoint out of her blazer pocket, turns her left hand over and writes {水|Wednesday} on the inside of her wrist, small, just under her cuff.
"Excuse me. Mizuno-san?"
Nanoha's standing by my desk with her lunch held in front of her in both hands, the way she holds things when she's about to do something brave.
"Oh—hi. You're…"
"Tachibana Nanoha. Um— I sit two rows over."
"If you'd like… I could show you around after school? The library, the music rooms. Which shoe lockers stick. Which vending machine eats coins. That kind of thing."
For a second Mizuno doesn't say anything.
"…Really?"
"It's not a big tour. The vending machine part is the most important."
"I'd love that. Which one eats coins?"
"Oh, and call me Natsuki."
"…Natsuki-san."
"Eh, 'san'? We're the same age!"
"I'm working up to it."
"Okay, okay. Then I'll call you Nanoha. All right? I'm doing it anyway."
"That's—yes. That's fine."
Mizuno laughs, and after a second Nanoha does too, ducking her head over her lunch. The two of them in the window light, over the top of my head. I feel like furniture.
I eat my rice. It's good rice. I made it myself.
Natsuki noticed everything.

That was the first thing Nanoha learned on the tour. Natsuki noticed that the stairs by the art room squeaked on the fourth step and the eleventh. She noticed that the third-floor girls' bathroom had a window that looked straight at the mountains, and she said "Oh," softly, like she'd been handed something.
They ended the tour in their own empty classroom, the evening sun coming in sideways and turning every desk gold. Natsuki leaned back against the desk in front of her own.
"Serious question. Is this building haunted? Something in the music room was knocking."
"It's old. The pipes sound like a ghost."
"Perfect."
"So. What about you and Fujisawa?"
"Me and Kōhei?"
"You live next door, right? Somebody said."
"Since we were born."
"No way. Real childhood friends? Baby pictures and everything?"
"Real childhood friends."
Nanoha said it as lightly as she knew how. She'd had practice.
"I've never stayed anywhere long enough to have one of those. You know? Someone who knows which drawer sticks in your kitchen."
Nanoha didn't say that Kōhei's kitchen drawer stuck. She didn't say she'd known it since she was six.
"Hey. Does Fujisawa ever compete up north? Around Sendai?"
"Not that I know of. Why?"
"I feel like I've met him somewhere before. I just can't place it."
"I have met him before. Every day. For sixteen years."
"Ha— okay. Then it's his face. He's got kind of a normal one, right? Don't tell him I said that."
"Thanks for today, Nanoha. Seriously. First days are usually…"
She didn't finish. She just smiled, and it was a different smile from the one she'd used in front of the class. Smaller. It looked like it cost her something.
"Anyway. Thanks."
Somewhere between the library and the gym, Nanoha had decided that she liked Mizuno Natsuki.
She'd decided it firmly, the way you shut a window against the wind.
She did not let herself think about why it had needed deciding at all.
I'm taking the burnables out to the corner. Pickup moved to Tuesdays and Fridays last fall. Dad's handwriting on the whiteboard still says Monday, and tonight I went with the handwriting.
That's when Nanoha comes up the street with her school bag over her shoulder, back from walking Mizuno home to her place by the station.
"You're taking out the trash on the wrong day."
"I'm moving it closer to the right day. How was the tour?"
"Good. She noticed the squeaky stairs. Both of them."
"Nobody notices the eleventh step."
"She did."
"She's nice, Kōhei. I like her."
"What did you think of her?"
"She seems fine."
"You smiled."
"When?"
"When she said she was looking for a dojo that would put up with her. You did your—"
She drops her chin and narrows her eyes. I think it's supposed to be me.
"I don't have a face."
"You have several. I've catalogued them. That one's number four. 'Somebody wants to fight me.'"
"What's number one?"
"Secret."
She walks the ten feet to her own front door. Pauses with her hand on the latch.
"Good night, Kō-chan."
"Night, Chibi."
The door closes.
A moment later her upstairs light comes on, in the window that faces mine across a gap so narrow you could pass a book through it if you leaned.
I stand there for a while longer than the garbage requires.
In bed I run my thumb over the callus on my left palm.
There's a dream I've had since I was small.
I never remember it properly when I wake. Only pieces.
Tonight, it comes back.
The sound of a river, close by.
My wrist stings. There's a cut on the inside of it, where a blade got past me in training, and I've held it closed the whole way home.
Somewhere above us, a branch moving in the wind.
Petals.
"You're late."
She says it like a scolding. She says it like she's laughing.
She says it like she's been waiting a very long time.
"Hurt again. Give me your hand… Hold still."
Hands that aren't mine wind a strip of cloth around a wrist that is. Slow and careful, like the knot matters more than anything else in the world.
And then I wake up, and the only thing left is a feeling I can't put a name to.
That someone was waiting for me.
That I kept them waiting far too long.

notes.karaage: Japanese fried chicken: bite-size pieces marinated in soy sauce, ginger and garlic, dusted in starch and deep-fried. A lunch-box staple, because it's still good cold.
notes.fusuma: A sliding door of thick paper over a wooden frame, used between rooms in a Japanese house.
notes.kinpira: Kinpira gobō: thin strips of burdock root and carrot, stir-fried, then cooked down in soy sauce, sugar and mirin (sweet rice wine). A classic make-ahead side dish that keeps for several days.
notes.taiyaki: A fish-shaped griddle cake (the name means "baked sea bream"), usually filled with sweet red-bean paste and sold hot from street stalls. Whether to start with the head or the tail is an old argument in Japan.
notes.shodan: First dan, the first rank above the beginner grades in kendo, earned at a formal grading exam (kendo has no belts; the rank comes as a certificate). Serious high-school players usually hold first or second dan.
